description_full: Companhia de Saneamento Básico do Estado de São Paulo - SABESP provides basic and environmental sanitation services in the São Paulo State, Brazil. It supplies treated water and sewage services on a wholesale basis. Companhia de Saneamento Básico do Estado de São Paulo - SABESP was founded in 1954 and is headquartered in São Paulo, Brazil.
ceo_bio: Mr. Carlos Augusto Leone Piani C.F.A. | CEO & Member of Executive Board | Age 52
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 9K people. Revenue per employee of $744K ranks in the bottom quartile among Utilities peers, with revenue growing 6%/yr across its filed history. Each employee generates $150K of free cash flow annually.
financial_summary: Companhia de saneamento Basico  is a large-cap utilities business with a $17.4B market cap on $6.7B of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +23% over the past three years, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder. Operating margins are expanding by +2.8pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.
Returns on capital run at 16% against a 9% cost of capital, a 7-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it, with gross margins sitting at 37%.

The business throws off $1.4B in free cash flow — roughly 20 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, with adequate 0.77× cash conversion.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.9× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 6.1×.

Shareholder yield is only 0.8%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 2.4× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 45% operating margin runs 24pp above the Utilities median (21%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 2.36x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
It accounts for 0.8% of sector revenue and 1.9% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+6.3% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 97 companies in the universe; the top four hold 26% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 22% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 31% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 47% and a beta of 0.72, it is more defensive than the market.
About $52.4M trades a day, enough to build a position, and interest is running hot at 1.9x its yearly average volume.
In past sell-offs it fell 62% in the 2020 crash, 30% in the 2022 bear market and 70% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 54% below its DCF fair value of $10.74, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 45%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $7.74 to $15.07 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Utilities peers: P/E 12.0 vs 20.3, EV/EBITDA 3.4 vs 12.6 and P/FCF 12.7 vs 20.0 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 3% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 7.9% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 5.6% (vs the 8% bar).
The 6 covering analysts target $6.31 on average, 28% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 16% earns above the cost of capital of 9.0%, but the 7pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.45).
It runs a 37% gross margin and converts 20% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality is a concern: cash conversion of only 0.77x.
ROE of 30% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.2x equity multiplier).
Operating margin is running 17pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 0.9x net debt to EBITDA ($272.4M of cash against $3.6B of debt), with interest covered 6.1x.
The current ratio of 0.89 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 23.0% over 3 years, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 17%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
It has missed earnings estimates by 9.0% on average.
Analysts expect 47.2% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.0%), and institutions hold 11%.
Shareholder yield is a modest 0.8% (0.6% in dividends).
It has paid a dividend for 14 consecutive years, though it has been cut 5.7% a year over the last five.
people: With about 9,057 employees, each generates about $744K of revenue, 0.7x the Utilities median, and revenue has grown 5.7% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $150K of free cash flow per employee.
